hero.name: Ayesha
hero.who: a design team supervisor at a Tiruppur garment exporter who leads with bonuses and fines

story.b: Ayesha runs a small design team at a garment exporter in Tiruppur. Her five designers create sample T-shirts and kurtas for buyers abroad. When orders slowed this year, the owner announced two thousand rupees for every approved sample and a fine for every missed deadline. Ayesha passed it on with a stern speech. Three months later, the team hits its deadlines, but every design looks like last season's safest ones with small colour changes. Nobody stays late to try a new print anymore. Even Ayesha, who got a raise last year, drags herself through Monday mornings. Then a buyer emails that the new collection feels tired. She reads it twice in the canteen over idli, wondering why more money has made everyone care less.

ask.q: The team now plays safe to win the bonus. What should Ayesha understand first?
o: The bonus is too small, so doubling it will inspire bolder designs
On creative work, rewards can narrow thinking, so the bonus may be part of the problem
The fines are too soft, so stricter penalties will push them harder
ask.why: Bigger rewards or harsher fines just push the same lever harder. For simple, routine work that can help, but creative work needs curiosity and risk-taking, and chasing a reward tends to shrink both. Seeing that the bonus itself narrows their thinking is the first step to fixing it.

chapters.take: Rewards can speed up simple work but quietly squeeze the life out of creative work.

story.b: Ayesha asks the owner for a meeting and proposes something unusual. Keep the bonus for the packing section, where the work is simple and counting cartons faster really helps. But for her designers, fold the sample bonus into a fair raise and drop the fines, so money is settled and off their minds. The owner frowns, worried they will slack, but agrees to try it for two months. At first the team is suspicious. Then Kumaresan, the quietest designer, brings in a print based on the kolam patterns his mother draws every morning. It is not safe at all. Two weeks earlier he would never have risked it for a bonus. A buyer in Spain picks it for a trial order, and Ayesha smiles all afternoon.

ask.q: The owner now wants to offer a big cash prize for the best design of the month. What should Ayesha advise?
o: Pay fairly and let curiosity drive design, keeping prizes for routine targets
Agree, since a bigger prize will surely push more creative work
Add a fine for the worst design so carrot and stick work together
ask.why: A big prize turns designing into a contest for money, which can make people play safe or copy what won before. Fines add fear, which shrinks creativity further. Fair pay settles the money question, so the designers' attention can go to the work itself.

chapters.take: Pay people fairly, then get money off their minds so the work can lead.

story.b: Ayesha has always checked every step. She chose the fabrics, approved each sketch and decided who worked with whom. For the new summer order she tries the opposite. She sets the goal clearly: eight pieces for a German buyer, within budget, by the twentieth. Then she lets the team decide the rest. Selvi asks to work seven to three, so she can collect her son from school. Kumaresan and Jency pair up on prints. Ayesha bites her tongue when their first sketches look strange. But the team starts arriving early on their own and arguing happily about colours. The collection is ready on the eighteenth, two days ahead, and it is the freshest work they have done in a year.

ask.q: A new designer keeps asking Ayesha to approve every small choice. How should Ayesha respond?
o: Keep approving each step, since new people need control to avoid mistakes
Give a clear goal and deadline, then let her decide how to reach it
Tell her to figure everything out alone, with no goal or check-in
ask.why: Approving every small choice keeps her dependent and dulls her effort. Leaving her with no goal at all is not freedom, just confusion. A clear target with freedom over how to get there gives her ownership, and ownership tends to bring out people's best work.

chapters.take: Set a clear goal, then give people a real say in how they get there.

story.b: Ayesha realises she herself stopped growing years ago. In design college in Coimbatore she drew beautifully. Now she mostly fills spreadsheets. So she picks one skill to get better at: drawing floral prints by hand. Every day after lunch she spends twenty minutes sketching, trying a flower slightly harder than yesterday's. The early sketches are clumsy, and she hides them in a drawer. By the third week her lines are looser and more confident. She notices those twenty minutes are the part of the day she looks forward to most. So she starts a Friday hour where each designer teaches the others one technique they are working to master. Jency begins with block printing. Nobody is paid extra, and nobody misses it.

ask.q: Selvi wants to improve at pattern cutting but feels slow and frustrated. What should Ayesha suggest?
o: Stick to the cuts she is already good at, so she feels confident
Try the most complicated pattern straight away to learn faster
Practise regularly on cuts a little harder than her current level
ask.why: Staying with easy cuts feels good but builds little, and jumping to the hardest pattern usually ends in frustration. Steady practice just beyond her current skill keeps her stretching and improving, and that slow, visible progress becomes its own reward over time.

chapters.take: Getting better at something that matters is one of the deepest rewards at work.

story.b: A charity in Ooty orders sweaters and T-shirts for a hill school where many children walk to class in the cold. It is a small, low-margin order, and the team treats it as routine. Ayesha calls the school and asks the headmistress to send a few photos of the children. She prints them and pins them on the board above the cutting tables. The mood changes. Kumaresan redesigns the collar so it will not scratch. Selvi suggests a pocket deep enough for a folded note from home. Nobody asks about extra pay. Weeks later, when photos arrive of the children wearing the T-shirts at assembly, the team crowds around Ayesha's phone. She sees what the bonus never gave them, a reason.

ask.q: The packing team says their job is just boxes and tape. What could help them feel their work matters?
o: Show them who receives the boxes and how careful packing helps those people
Tell them packing is simple, so they should not expect it to feel meaningful
Offer a small prize to whoever packs the most boxes this week
ask.why: Telling them the work cannot be meaningful closes the door, and a prize speeds up packing without giving it purpose. Seeing who opens those boxes, and how careful packing protects their order, links the task to real people. That sense of contribution tends to lift both care and mood.

chapters.take: When people see who their work helps, a task becomes a contribution.

story.b: In October, a bigger exporter offers Ayesha a job with much higher pay. The role is mostly reports and buyer calls, with no design at all. Her husband says take the money. Ayesha sits down with a notebook and writes three things she would happily do even if nobody paid her: drawing prints, teaching young designers, and watching a new collection come alive. The new job offers none of them. She does not pretend money is unimportant. Her son's college fees are coming. So she goes to her owner, shows him the offer, asks for a fair raise and explains honestly what keeps her here. The owner agrees to part of the raise. Ayesha stays, and this time she knows exactly why.

ask.q: Ayesha's nephew must choose between a well-paid job he finds dull and a slightly lower-paid one he finds exciting. What is wise advice?
o: Always take the highest pay, since interest fades but money lasts
Ignore pay completely and follow only what excites him
Weigh fair pay, but give real weight to work he would enjoy for its own sake
ask.why: Pay matters, especially with real bills, so ignoring it is unwise. But choosing only by salary can lead to years of draining work. Motivation that comes from enjoying the work itself tends to last longer, so it deserves serious weight next to a fair income.

chapters.take: Money matters, but work you enjoy for its own sake keeps you going longer.

story.b: By spring, Ayesha's team has sent out their boldest collection in years, and two new buyers have placed orders. The designers still earn fair pay, but nobody talks about bonuses at lunch now. They talk about prints. Selvi leaves at three and often finishes first. The Friday skill hour has grown to include two people from the packing section who wanted to learn sketching. The photos of the hill school children are still pinned above the cutting tables. Ayesha's own floral sketches now appear in real samples. On Monday mornings she no longer drags herself in. She walks through the gate early, with a filter coffee and a new idea she cannot wait to try.

chapters.take: People do their best work with freedom, growth and a reason that matters.
